opening.headline: When LLM call costs suddenly increase, you learn how to isolate and identify which team's specific feature is responsible.
body: Let's consider that LLM call costs have noticeably increased since last week. Simply looking at the total amount on the invoice does not reveal which team or model is responsible for the increase. Since costs are derived from token count and model pricing, to identify the root cause, we need to break down each call's token records by model, application, and team.

In this class, we examine what ml_obs metrics are generated within LLM spans, and how cost_tags—tags attached to spans that express costs in terms of cost and token metrics—can be used to allocate expenses by team or function. Finally, we review a case where root cause tracing was difficult due to the absence of tags, and establish criteria for determining which tags to apply and how to apply them.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the role of ml_obs metrics and cost_tags
Tag settings can be read to analyze the cause of cost analysis being blocked.

screens.title: The cost has suddenly increased, but I don't know who's responsible.
screens.lead: First, let's examine a scene where the root cause cannot be determined solely based on total cost. Consider the graph and question marks in the diagram and think about what criteria to use for splitting the data.

visual.alt: A bar chart showing LLM costs at the weekly level spikes in the final week, with three question marks beneath it asking about team, model, and request.

paragraphs: LLM call costs have noticeably increased since last week. Monthly invoices or total amount graphs indicate that costs have risen, but they do not specify which team or which model is responsible.

The cost comes from the number of tokens and the model price per unit. Therefore, to identify the cause, we need to have a record of each request's token usage, and we must be able to break down those records by model, application, or request unit. Without a clear breakdown criterion, we're left with having to manually open and inspect each trace individually.
This course covers the ml_obs metrics generated by Datadog in LLM spans, and cost_tags that break down costs by teams or features based on our own criteria.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: The fact that the total amount has increased is different from the information about who caused the increase. Without pre-defining the criteria for splitting the data, it becomes how difficult it is to identify the root cause later, as demonstrated in the case studies at the end of the lesson.

screens.outro: First, let's recall the basis on which we're currently dividing costs.

screens.title: Have you ever split the costs by team?
screens.lead: When you select a hint, the instructor's thought process is displayed. Since you haven't entered an answer yet, first consider how it might look in our environment before clicking it.

items.prompt: Is there an indicator showing which team's call it is?
items.answer: Having only one app name is insufficient to distinguish between teams when the same app is shared across multiple teams. To enable future cost allocation based on teams, team names or feature names must be preserved at the time of invocation. The cost_tags in this lesson precisely achieve this by using such identifiers as cost indicators.

items.prompt: If we attach a value like a team name as a tag, how many types of values can we have?
items.answer: Team names or function names are limited in variety. However, when user IDs or request IDs are attached as tags, the number of possible values expands without bound. The number of distinct values a tag can take is called cardinality, and cost metrics must only include tags with a limited number of value types.

items.prompt: What criteria are used to trigger alerts regarding cost increases?
items.answer: Sending alerts based on total costs can cause one team's sudden increase in usage to be obscured by the usual consumption of other teams. By monitoring by tag, each team can receive separate alerts when their respective thresholds are exceeded. For this to work, the tag must first be mapped to a cost metric.

screens.outro: With the benchmark in mind, let's first examine the ml_obs metrics provided natively by Datadog.

screens.title: ml_obs metric: cost, tokens, latency, error
screens.lead: The following table lists representative ml_obs metrics generated within an LLM span. Read the names from the end to the beginning to understand what specific metric each name represents.

data.notes: These metrics are generated within LLM spans and are calculated based on 100% traffic. They are retained according to Datadog's standard retention policy and remain available for 15 months, allowing viewing in dashboards, monitors, and notebooks. Default tags include env, ml_app, model_name, model_provider, service, and version. Tags that are specific to spans cannot be used as tags for metrics by default. In contrast, per-request original values retained in spans follow the default trace retention period of 15 days, enabling older cost trends to be viewed as metrics. Costs are automatically calculated based on token counts and the provider's published pricing, and direct values can be entered if pricing differs. When entering values directly, they must be input in U.S. dollars, but are stored in nanodollars.

screens.outro: Basic tags do not allow us to differentiate teams, so now we'll look at how to establish our own criteria using cost_tags.

screens.title: cost_tags: tags that break down costs by team
screens.lead: Move the slider to compare cases where no tags are assigned, where only a team tag is assigned, and where both team and feature tags are assigned. You can verify how well the cost graph divides when code changes occur.

visual.alt: Tagless, team tags, team and feature tags in three states: a chart divided into one, team-specific, team and feature-specific cost bars.

stops.body: This is a case where no tag has been assigned at the call site. The only basis for viewing cost metrics are the basic tags such as `ml_app`, `model_name`, and `model_provider`. If three teams are using the same `ml_app` tag, the graph will display only a single bar, and it will not be possible to determine which team increased their costs. In this state, the only option is to open each trace individually for inspection.

At the call site, attach a team tag to the span and specify its key in cost_tags.

``
LLMObs.annotate(
    tags={"team": "search"},
    cost_tags=["team"],
)
```

`tags` is a parameter used to assign values to a span, and `cost_tags` is a parameter used to select keys that should be associated with cost and token metrics. Python uses `cost_tags`, while Node.js uses `costTags`. Once `ml_obs.span.llm.total.cost` is grouped by team, the data will be segmented by team. Keys present in tags but absent in cost_tags will not be associated with cost metrics and thus cannot be used for grouping by those keys.

If we raise the baseline further, we can see which features consume costs within a team.

```
LLMObs.annotate(
    tags={"team": "search", "feature": "summary"},
    cost_tags=["team", "feature"],
)
```

By filtering the metric `ml_app` and grouping by team and feature, the bar chart breaks down again by feature. In the Cost Overview, you can also view total expenditures by app, provider, and custom tag. Setting up monitoring by tag allows you to receive separate alerts when thresholds are exceeded per team.

The tags to be added to cost_tags must have limited value types. Examples include `team`, `customer_tier`, and `feature`. Tags with high cardinality where values continuously increase—such as user IDs or request IDs—may result in some data being truncated or lost in metrics. Additionally, custom tags apply only to cost and token metrics and are not attached to other span metrics such as `ml_obs.span.duration`.

screens.outro: Now that we know how to assign and select tags, let's apply this to a case where no tags were previously assigned.

screens.title: Case Explanation: When no team tags are available, root cause tracing becomes difficult.
screens.lead: The instructor breaks down a case where costs doubled within a month, step by step. Select the next arrow to see how the data is split, where it gets stuck, and how to fix it.

visual.alt: A side-by-side comparison between a cost graph without tags and a cost graph with team tags.

steps.title: Situation: Costs doubled in one month
steps.body: Within a month, LLM costs have doubled. Three teams are sharing the same `ml_app`, so the app-level graph appears as a single bar. We need to investigate the cause of the cost increase.

steps.title: Divide into stages by model axis
steps.body: We divided by the base tag `model_name`. We can observe that certain large models have increased in prominence. However, we do not know which team started using those models more extensively.

steps.title: Stage 2 limit: Cannot distinguish teams by app axis.
steps.body: `ml_app` Since there is only one instance, teams cannot be distinguished by app. All criteria available for splitting by basic tags have been exhausted, and the remaining method is to manually inspect each trace. This approach is slow, and traces are retained for only the default 15 days, making it impossible to locate older calls.

steps.title: Step 3, First Attempt to Read: Incorrectly Attached Tags
steps.body: The team tried tagging it. They applied tags `tags={"team": "search", "request_id": rid}` and `cost_tags=["request_id"]`, but the team did not appear in the graph, and the values were cut off or lost. There is a mismatch between the two.

steps.title: Step 4: Cause and Correction
steps.body: The request ID may be truncated or lost in cost metrics due to its high cardinality nature. Additionally, `team` exists only in tags and not in cost_tags, so it does not appear in cost metrics. It is corrected to `cost_tags=["team"]`. Tags are attached at the call site that creates a span.

steps.title: Stage 5 Reanalysis
steps.body: Now let's group `ml_obs.span.llm.total.cost` by team. The increase can be directly observed in the graph as originating from a team's summary feature. If needed, you can further narrow it down to a feature level.

steps.title: 6-step governance: Establish the rules
steps.body: Defines rules that specify which tags are mandatory. For criteria with limited values such as team, feature, or customer tier, the same key name is applied at each call point. Access control can be divided by team scope using the `ml_app` tag.

steps.title: Conclusion: The tag is resolved at the call site beforehand.
steps.body: Tags must be attached at the call site and placed into cost_tags in order to track costs at the team level. Once a problem occurs, it cannot be split based on a baseline that was not previously recorded. Baselines that you want to split must be predefined and preseeded.

screens.outro: We have completed the example; now I will summarize the key points and conclude.

screens.title: Key takeaway: Unlabeled costs cannot be tracked
screens.lead: We summarize the course content as a single flow. Begin by recalling the sudden cost graph from the opening scene and read through it.

paragraphs: The ml_obs metric is a Datadog metric generated within an LLM span, displaying tokens, costs, latency, and errors relative to 100% traffic. Like standard Datadog metrics, it is retained for 15 months, enabling long-term trend visualization on dashboards and monitors even after traces are deleted after 15 days. The cost metric is measured in nanodollars.

To split costs by team or function, values must be attached to tags at the call site, and the keys representing cost and token metrics must be specified in the cost_tags. Only the keys specified in cost_tags will be attached to cost and token metrics; they will not be attached to other span metrics.

An uplift tag must have a limited type of value. High cardinality values such as user ID or request ID may be truncated or lost. Costs without tags cannot be traced later, so the criteria you want to split on should be predefined and attached at the call site. Adopting this practice ensures you won't be overwhelmed when costs spike later and total cost graphs become difficult to interpret.

callout.text: When costs increase, first separate the model and app using basic tags, and if team or feature-based grouping is needed, verify whether both the tag and cost_tag share the same key and whether the value types are restricted.

glossary.def: Prefix for Datadog metrics generated from an LLM span, containing span count, errors, tokens, latency, and cost.
This is a parameter in a span that specifies the keys to be included in cost and token metrics. In Node.js, it is named costTags.
The estimated cost indicator uses units of one hundred-millionth of a dollar.
The number of different values a tag can have. If values continue indefinitely, it is said to have high cardinality.
Rules defining how data should be handled, such as access control, masking, and retention periods.

misconceptions.myth: When a tag is attached to a span, it is automatically appended to the cost metric as well.
misconceptions.fact: The span itself does not become a default tag for metrics. To attach tags to cost and token metrics, the key must be specified using cost_tags.
Tags whose values endlessly increase, like user IDs, may be truncated or omitted from metrics. Only tags with a limited set of values should be included.

misconceptions.myth: Indicators and span data are stored for the same period.
misconceptions.fact: The ml_obs metric is retained for 15 months, while traces and spans are retained by default for 15 days. Older traces are verified through metrics.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: Untracked costs cannot be traced later.
The ml_obs metric displays token, cost, latency, and error rates based on 100% traffic volume and is retained for 15 months.
Only the keys posted in cost_tags are attached to the cost and token metrics.
The tag being raised must be a key with a restricted type of value, such as team or feature.
The original values per request follow the trace retention period, while metrics remain for a longer duration.
